A Note on Single-Server QPIR from One-Way Functions

                Prabhanjan Ananth‗              Divyanshu Bhardwaj†                 Aditya Gulati‡
                      UCSB                            UCSB                             UCSB


                                                      Abstract
       We observe that there exists a single-server quantum private information retrieval with polylogarithmic
       communication assuming post-quantum one-way functions. Our observation follows immediately from
       the compilation technique of [Kerenidis-Wolf STOC’03] when combined with distributed point functions
       by [Gilboa-Ishai EUROCRYPT’14].


1     Introduction
Classical PIR. Private information retrieval (PIR), introduced by Chor, Goldreich, Kushilevitz, and Su-
dan [5], allows a client to retrieve a designated bit D[i] from a database D ∈ {0, 1}N without revealing
the index i to the server. In the standard single-server setting, information-theoretic privacy requires lin-
ear communication, and hence any nontrivial communication saving necessarily relies on computational
assumptions. Such protocols are referred to as computational private information retrieval (CPIR) protocols.
Kushilevitz and Ostrovsky gave the first sublinear-communication single-server CPIR protocol under the
quadratic residuosity assumption [9], and Cachin, Micali, and Stadler subsequently obtained polyloga-
rithmic communication under the Φ-hiding assumption [4]. Döttling, Garg, Ishai, Malavolta, Mour and
Ostrovsky designed CPIR protocols with polylogarithmic communication from decisional Diffie Hellman
assumption or the quadratic residousity assumption.
    Brakerski and Vaikuntanathan later constructed an asymptotically efficient single-server CPIR protocol
from the Learning With Errors (LWE) assumption [11]. More recently, Abram, Malavolta, and Roy gave the
first nontrivial CPIR construction from a code-based assumption, relying on the quasi-polynomial hardness
of low-noise Learning Parity with Noise (LPN) [12]. Beimel, Ishai, Kushilevitz, and Malkin showed that
one-way functions are necessary for any nontrivial communication saving in single-server PIR [3], while
Ishai, Kushilevitz, and Ostrovsky showed that every one-round single-server CPIR protocol with sub-linear
communication implies collision-resistant hash functions [14]. Thus, in the standard no-preprocessing
model, single-server CPIR is known from number-theoretic, lattice-based, and code-based assumptions,
whereas one-way functions constitute a necessary lower bound on the required assumptions.

Quantum PIR. A few works have explored the possibility of using quantum communication to achieve
private information retrieval. Kerenidis and de Wolf used quantum interference to convert two classical
queries into one quantum query and derived applications to locally decodable codes and PIR [7]; they
also constructed quantum symmetrically private PIR protocols √   [8]. For a single honest server, Le Gall
gave an information-theoretically private QPIR protocol with O( N ) qubits of communication [10]. This
positive result is sensitive to the adversarial model: Baumeler and Broadbent proved that single-server
QPIR requires linear communication against specious servers, the quantum analogue of honest-but-curious
adversaries [2]. Aharonov, Brakerski, Chung, Green, Lai, and Sattath further isolated the input-purification

Main Theorem.       The main theorem is as follows:

Theorem 1.1. There exists a single-server private information retrieval protocol:
    • assuming post-quantum one-way functions,
    • with one round of quantum communication,
    • with communication complexity that is polylogarithmic in N , where N is the size of the database.

In the above theorem, we consider databases where each entry is a single bit. Although the central quantum
idea is not new, its combination with modern computational PIR constructions does not appear to have been
stated explicitly in the literature.

2.1    Quantum Private Information Retrieval
A one-round single-server quantum CPIR protocol consists of the following quantum polynomial time
algorithms:
    • Share(1λ , i): on input a security parameter λ and an index i ∈ [N ], it outputs a quantum state ρQE .

    • Eval(D, σQ ): on input a database D ∈ {0, 1}N and a quantum state σQ , it outputs a quantum state ξA .
    • Reconstruct: on input the registers E and A, it outputs y.
The client on input an index i ∈ [N ], computes ρQE ← Share(1λ , i). It sends the register Q to the server.
The server computes ξA ← Eval(D, σQ ), where σQ is the reduced density matrix on Q, and sends this to the
client. Finally, the client computes Reconstruct on the registers A and E to obtain the decoded answer D[i].

2.2   2-Server CPIR with Additive Reconstruction
A 2-server CPIR protocol consists of the following probabilistic polynomial time algorithms:
  • Share(1λ , i): on input a security parameter λ and an index i ∈ [N ], it outputs two strings (a0 , a1 ) along
    with a private state sti . We assume without loss of generality that |a0 | = |a1 |.
  • Eval(b, D, ab ): on input a bit b, a database D ∈ {0, 1}N and a string ab , it outputs a bit zb . This algorithm
    is a deterministic polynomial time algorithm.
  • Reconstruct(sti , z0 , z1 ): on input a private state sti , answers z0 , z1 and outputs the answer y.


   The client, on input an index i ∈ [N ], computes ((a0 , a1 ), st) ← Share(1λ , i). It sends a0 to the first
server and a1 to the second server. The first server computes z0 ← Eval(0, D, a0 ) and the second server
computes z1 ← Eval(1, D, a1 ). The servers respectively send z0 and z1 to the client. The client then computes
Reconstruct(st, z0 , z1 ) to obtain D[i].

Additive Reconstruction Property.         For every D ∈ {0, 1}N , every i ∈ [N ], and every ((a0 , a1 ), st) in the
support of Share(1λ , i),

                        Reconstruct(st, z0 , z1 ) := Eval(0, D, a0 ) ⊕ Eval(1, D, a1 ) = D[i].

We can consider the relaxation of the above condition, where the correctness only holds with probability

Communication Complexity.          The total number of bits exchanged between the server and the client is

Theorem 2.1 (Gilboa–Ishai [6]; post-quantum instantiation). There exists a two-server (classical) computational
PIR protocol:

     • assuming post-quantum one-way functions,
     • with one round of classical communication,
     • with additive reconstruction (over F2 ),
     • with 1-bit answers and with communication complexity polylogarithmic in N .

Justification of Theorem 2.1. Gilboa and Ishai construct a distributed point function (DPF): on input i,
its key-generation algorithm outputs two short keys (a0 , a1 ) whose pointwise evaluations xor to the unit
vector ei , while either key individually hides i. Taking the inner product of each expanded DPF share
with D gives answer bits z0 , z1 satisfying z0 ⊕ z1 = D[i]. Their construction is based on pseudorandom
generators. Instantiating it with a quantum-secure pseudorandom generator gives security against quantum
polynomial-time distinguishers; such pseudorandomness can be based on post-quantum one-way functions
via standard black-box transformations.
